C4 model.name: C4 model
C4 model.what: A hierarchical way to describe software architecture in four zoom levels — context, containers, components and code — with a small, consistent notation.
how: Draw the system context: the system, its users and the external systems
Zoom into containers: deployable or runnable units and how they talk
Zoom into components only where risk justifies it
Rarely go to code level; let the code speak
Add supporting views — runtime (dynamic) and deployment

items: System, people, external systems — for everyone
Apps, services, stores — for technical people
Parts inside a container — for its builders
Classes and tables — usually generated, if at all

pitfalls: Every container drawn to component level
Boxes without responsibilities or owners

arc42.name: arc42
arc42.what: A pragmatic template for communicating and documenting software architecture in twelve sections.
how: Use the sections as a checklist, not a form to fill
Add views and decisions as they are made
Keep it in the repository next to the code
arc42.use: Structuring the architecture description and baseline.

ISO/IEC 25010.name: ISO/IEC 25010
ISO/IEC 25010.what: ISO/IEC 25010:2023 Systems and software Quality Requirements and Evaluation (SQuaRE) — Product quality model. Defines the characteristics that make a product fit for use.
how: Pick the quality characteristics that matter for this product
Make each one measurable (target, how measured)
Use them to judge feasibility and to design and verify later
says: Product quality is described by nine characteristics, each with sub-characteristics
Quality requirements should be specified and measured, not assumed
The model is used to specify, measure and evaluate quality
ISO/IEC 25010.applies: In DISCOVER it is used during the feasibility rating (1.5.2) to surface which quality attributes would make the solution hard or costly.
ISO/IEC 25010.use: When judging feasibility and later when specifying non-functional requirements.
pitfalls: Listing all nine as 'important'

Architecture baseline.name: Architecture baseline
Architecture baseline.what: The versioned, agreed description of a system's architecture that builders work against and changes update deliberately.
how: Establish context, structure, boundaries, quality attributes, decisions

Ask before you build.name: Ask before you build
Ask before you build.what: An unclear criterion is a question for the product owner, not a guess in the code.

dos: Log the question with who must answer
Clarify the criterion, not just your understanding

Understand before solving.name: Understand before solving
Understand before solving.what: Don't design anything until the context, constraints and people are understood.

donts: Propose solutions in the first meeting

Facts are sourced, guesses are labelled.name: Facts are sourced, guesses are labelled
Facts are sourced, guesses are labelled.what: Every statement about the system is either a fact with a source you could show someone, or an assumption labelled as one, with a confidence and a way to test it.
how: Write the source next to every fact
Tag anything without a source as an assumption
Give each assumption a confidence and a test
Promote an assumption to a fact only with evidence

dos: “The import API takes 500 lines a request (ERP guide §7.3)”
“A-01, low confidence: most PDFs are generated — test on the inbox sample”
donts: “Most orders are PDFs” with no source

Facts are sourced, guesses are labelled.use: All of technical discovery, and every review of it.

Brief decomposition.name: Brief decomposition
Brief decomposition.what: Breaking a client brief into the things an engineer can reason about: capabilities, inputs and outputs, users and volumes, the scope edge and the open questions.
how: Rewrite the ask as one sentence with a verb and no technology
List the capabilities it implies, as verbs
List every input and output with its format
Note users and volumes, each with a source
Draw the scope edge both ways
Turn everything you can't answer into a question with an owner
Brief decomposition.use: The first hour with any brief, before opening the code.
pitfalls: Choosing the technology in the first sentence
Copying the brief's numbers without their source
Leaving the out-of-scope list empty

Data flow diagramming.name: Data flow diagramming
Data flow diagramming.what: Draws processes, data stores, external entities and the flows between them, with trust boundaries — the base for threat and privacy modelling.

Codebase walkthrough.name: Codebase walkthrough
Codebase walkthrough.what: A structured first read of an unfamiliar system: get it running, follow one real request end to end, then measure what you see.
how: Get read access and run it locally or in a test environment
Read the README, build files and dependency manifest
Follow one real transaction from entry point to database and back
Sketch the components you passed through
Measure: tests, coverage, dependency age, build steps, open issues
Write down what surprised you — that's where the risk is
Codebase walkthrough.use: Auditing an existing system before proposing changes to it.
pitfalls: Reading files alphabetically instead of following a request
Judging code health by feel instead of numbers
Trusting the documentation over the running system

API contract review.name: API contract review
API contract review.what: Checking an interface you'll depend on before you design around it: what it accepts, how you authenticate, its limits and what happens when it fails.
how: Find the real contract — OpenAPI spec, vendor guide or the code
Record limits: rate, payload size, timeouts, opening hours
Note error responses and whether calls are idempotent
Make one real call in a test environment
Log every gap as a question or a spike

rows: Spec or doc link and version
One real call made, with the response

API contract review.use: Every external system on the integration inventory.
pitfalls: Assuming limits from another vendor's API
Never making a real call before the design review

Context diagram.name: Context diagram
Context diagram.what: Shows the system as one box in the middle with the people and systems it exchanges information with.
how: Draw the system as a single box
Add external actors and systems around it
Label the flows in and out

Coding agent.name: Coding agent
Coding agent.what: An AI agent that reads and writes code in the repository, runs tests and proposes changes — on a branch, for a person to review.
how: Brief it with the story, criteria and ADRs
Let it work on a branch

Static analysis tool.name: Static analysis tool
Static analysis tool.what: Runs linters, analysers and SAST rules over the code and reports findings to the PR.

Document repository.name: Document repository
Document repository.what: A versioned store for briefs, logs and supporting documents.
how: One folder per initiative and stage

Problem / solution separation.name: Problem / solution separation
Problem / solution separation.what: Records a requested solution separately from the problem it implies, so the problem can be validated on its own.
how: Write the proposed solution exactly as asked
Ask what problem it would fix
Write the problem in solution-free words
Note the evidence you have, and what's still open

rows: Users re-type data into another system

Problem / solution separation.use: Whenever an idea arrives as a feature request.

Question backlog.name: Question backlog
Question backlog.what: A prioritised list of what discovery must learn, each question linked to a hypothesis.
how: Prioritise by value of the answer

Code review.name: Code review
Code review.what: A colleague reads a change before it merges, judging it against the story's criteria, the design and the team's standards.
how: Read the story and criteria first
Comment with file and line, kind and reason
Approve, request changes or ask for rework

rows: Does it do what the criteria say?
Does it follow the ADRs and module boundaries?
Is each criterion and failure case tested?
Will the next person understand it?

Evidence over assertion.name: Evidence over assertion
Evidence over assertion.what: A sentence is not evidence; every release criterion links to the artifact that proves it, for this build.
how: Link an artifact to every criterion
Check it names the release build

dos: Link the test run for the release build

Technical debt quadrant.name: Technical debt quadrant
Technical debt quadrant.what: Classifies debt by whether it was deliberate or inadvertent and prudent or reckless — which tells you how to talk about it and how to prevent more.
how: Place each debt item in a quadrant
Prevent the reckless kinds at the source

q: Deliberate–prudent: 'ship now, deal with it later'
Inadvertent–prudent: 'now we know how we should have done it'

Diagram-as-code.name: Diagram-as-code
Diagram-as-code.what: Writes architecture diagrams as text kept in the repository (e.g. Structurizr DSL, Mermaid, PlantUML).

OpenAPI Specification.name: OpenAPI Specification
OpenAPI Specification.what: A machine-readable format for describing HTTP APIs — operations, parameters, schemas, errors and security — from which docs, clients and tests can be generated.
how: Review it as an interface decision
Generate reference docs and contract tests from it
says: An API is described in a language-agnostic, machine-readable document
The description is the single source for docs and tooling
OpenAPI Specification.applies: In BUILD the contract drives contract tests (4.5.3) and the generated API reference (4.6.2).
OpenAPI Specification.use: For every HTTP API a team provides.

Data contract.name: Data contract
Data contract.what: A versioned agreement on the shape, meaning, quality and freshness of data one owner provides to readers.

Dependency mapping.name: Dependency mapping
Dependency mapping.what: Lists everything that depends on an item — users, systems, reports, contracts and data flows — before changing or retiring it.
how: Add consumers from logs and access lists
pitfalls: Relying only on the CMDB

Surface unknowns early.name: Surface unknowns early
Surface unknowns early.what: List what you don't know before estimating or committing.

Data lineage mapping.name: Data lineage mapping
Data lineage mapping.what: Traces each data item from source through transformations to every destination and store.
how: Mark third parties and personal data

API documentation generator.name: API documentation generator
API documentation generator.what: Generates browsable API reference from an OpenAPI contract.

Assumption log.name: Assumption log
Assumption log.what: A running list of assumptions, each tagged with its source, confidence and how it will be validated.
how: Write each assumption as a statement
Assumption log.use: Whenever context or constraints are captured.

Assumption mapping.name: Assumption mapping
Assumption mapping.what: Lists assumptions, then plots them by importance and evidence to choose what to test first.
how: Plot on the importance × evidence map

Impact analysis.name: Impact analysis
Impact analysis.what: Working out which parts of the system a change can affect, to choose regression scope.

Assumption map.name: Assumption map
Assumption map.what: A 2×2 that plots assumptions by how important they are and how much evidence exists, revealing which to test first.
how: List every assumption behind the idea
Place each by importance (if wrong, does it kill the idea?)
Place each by evidence (do we already know?)
Test the important, unevidenced ones first
Assumption map.use: Before choosing what to research or experiment on.
Assumption map.source: David J. Bland, Testing Business Ideas

Lean Product Discovery.name: Lean Product Discovery
Lean Product Discovery.what: A way of reducing the risk of building the wrong thing by testing value, usability, feasibility and viability with small, fast experiments before committing engineering effort.
how: List the assumptions behind the idea
Rank them by risk — what would kill it if wrong?
Pick the cheapest test that would expose the riskiest one
Run it and read the result against a pre-set bar
Persevere, pivot or stop — then test the next risk

rows: Can they figure out how to use it?
Can we build it with what we have?
Does it work for the business?

Lean Product Discovery.use: Before committing a team to build anything new.
pitfalls: Testing the easy assumptions instead of the risky ones
Calling a demo to stakeholders 'validation'

Spike.name: Spike
Spike.what: A short, timeboxed piece of throwaway work that answers one specific technical question.
how: Build only enough to answer it
Record the answer and the decision; discard the code

items: One question, answerable yes / no or with a number

Spike.use: When feasibility depends on an unknown.

Technical spike.name: Technical spike
Technical spike.what: Engineers build a throwaway proof to answer one feasibility question within a fixed timebox.
how: Build the minimum to answer it
Report the answer and the remaining unknowns

Make beliefs falsifiable.name: Make beliefs falsifiable
Make beliefs falsifiable.what: Write beliefs so that evidence could prove them wrong.
how: State what result would disprove it

donts: Write vague beliefs that can't fail

Learn the most for the least.name: Learn the most for the least
Learn the most for the least.what: Prioritise the questions that reduce the most uncertainty per unit of effort.
how: Rank questions by uncertainty removed ÷ cost

Hypothesis-driven development.name: Hypothesis-driven development
Hypothesis-driven development.what: Treats every idea as a hypothesis with a test and a measurable success signal.

structure.text: We believe [this capability / change] will result in [this outcome]. We will know we have succeeded when we see [this measurable signal].

Attribute-Driven Design.name: Attribute-Driven Design
Attribute-Driven Design.what: A method-framework that drives architecture design from ranked quality-attribute scenarios rather than from functions.
how: Review the inputs: drivers, constraints, concerns
Pick the highest-ranked drivers for this iteration
Choose design concepts (patterns, tactics) that satisfy the drivers
Attribute-Driven Design.use: Quality Attribute Specification (3.6) and Architecture Definition (3.3).

Five Whys.name: Five Whys
Five Whys.what: Ask 'why?' about five times to move from a symptom to its root cause.
how: Stop at a cause you can act on

Utility tree.name: Utility tree
Utility tree.what: Refines 'utility' into quality characteristics, refinements and ranked scenarios.

Solution-to-problem laddering.name: Solution-to-problem laddering
Solution-to-problem laddering.what: Climbs from 'we need X' to 'because Y happens' until a solution-free problem appears.

Causes over symptoms.name: Causes over symptoms
Causes over symptoms.what: Keep digging until the cause is found; complaints are symptoms.

dos: Trace each pain to a cause

Quality attribute scenarios.name: Quality attribute scenarios
Quality attribute scenarios.what: A six-part way of stating a quality requirement so it is testable: source, stimulus, environment, artifact, response and response measure.
how: Name the stimulus and its source
Quality attribute scenarios.use: Quantifying NFRs in PLAN; elaborated in DESIGN.
Quality attribute scenarios.source: Bass, Clements & Kazman, Software Architecture in Practice (SEI)

Fitness functions.name: Fitness functions
Fitness functions.what: Automated checks that measure an architectural characteristic — such as coupling, latency or use of a deprecated API — so modernisation progress and erosion are visible.
how: Write an automated check with a threshold
Run it in the pipeline or on a schedule
Fail the build or alert when it regresses

items: e.g. no calls to ERP API v2

Fitness functions.use: Proving debt is paid and stays paid.
Fitness functions.source: Ford, Parsons & Kua, Building Evolutionary Architectures (2017)

Measure what users feel.name: Measure what users feel
Measure what users feel.what: SLIs measure the user's experience — orders drafted, lines right — not server internals.
how: Measure at the edge users touch

donts: Alert on CPU as if it were an outage

Goal–Question–Metric.name: Goal–Question–Metric
Goal–Question–Metric.what: Derives metrics top-down: state the goal, ask the questions that show whether it is met, then choose the metrics that answer them.
how: Pick metrics that answer each question

items: How long does an order take now?
Median minutes, email received → order in ERP

Goal–Question–Metric.use: Turning success criteria into metric definitions.

Timebox.name: Timebox
Timebox.what: Fixes the time allowed and lets scope flex, forcing teams to prioritise what matters most.
how: Set the duration and end date
List the questions or work in priority order
Work top-down; stop at the end date
Review what was learned; decide what's next

Walking skeleton.name: Walking skeleton
Walking skeleton.what: The thinnest possible implementation that runs end to end through every major component, built first to prove the path.
how: Make it flow through every component end to end
Walking skeleton.use: The first slice of a new system or integration.
pitfalls: Building one layer fully before connecting the rest

Kepner-Tregoe problem analysis.name: Kepner-Tregoe problem analysis
Kepner-Tregoe problem analysis.what: A structured way to find a cause by comparing where the problem IS with where it COULD BE but IS NOT.
how: Describe the problem: what, where, when, extent
For each, record IS and IS NOT
Find what is distinctive about the IS side
Test causes that explain every IS and IS NOT
Kepner-Tregoe problem analysis.use: Diagnosis in incidents and problem investigations.

Fishbone diagram.name: Fishbone diagram
Fishbone diagram.what: Groups possible causes of a problem into categories along a 'fish skeleton' to find root causes.
how: Write the problem at the head
Dig into the likeliest with Five Whys

Sequence diagram.name: Sequence diagram
Sequence diagram.what: Shows the messages between participants over time for one scenario, including failure paths.

Root cause analysis.name: Root cause analysis
Root cause analysis.what: Finding where and why a defect was introduced so the cause, not just the instance, is fixed.
how: Ask why it was introduced and why it escaped
Fix the cause and the escape
Root cause analysis.use: Sev-1 and Sev-2 defects; recurring defect types.

Baseline measurement.name: Baseline measurement
Baseline measurement.what: Measuring today's numbers for each success metric from logs, data or timed samples, with a method another engineer can re-run.
how: Pick the metric and its definition
Choose the source — logs, database, timed sample
Pull a representative period (normal and peak)
Compute median and p95, and error rates
Write down the query or method, period and sample size
Baseline measurement.use: Before comparing options, and again in VERIFY and EVOLVE with the same method.
pitfalls: Averages hiding a slow tail
A quiet week used as the baseline

Reproduce before you fix.name: Reproduce before you fix
Reproduce before you fix.what: Make the problem happen on demand, in a safe environment, before you explain it or change anything.
how: Pick real (masked) samples or a recorded case
Write the steps so someone else can repeat them
Only then trace causes or try fixes

dos: “Reproduced on 20 masked inbox PDFs in the ERP test tenant — steps in the trace”
donts: “Users say it's slow, so we'll add caching”

Reproduce before you fix.use: The first step of any technical investigation.

Time-and-motion study.name: Time-and-motion study
Time-and-motion study.what: Timing real tasks before and after a change to measure its effect on effort.

Traceability matrix.name: Traceability matrix
Traceability matrix.what: A table linking each requirement to its stories, criteria, test cases and latest results, so coverage gaps are visible.
how: Link the latest run to each case
Highlight rows with no case or no passing run
Traceability matrix.use: Coverage review and the Quality Gate.

Log store.name: Log store
Log store.what: Central, searchable store of logs with retention rules.

Observability platform.name: Observability platform
Observability platform.what: Collects metrics, logs and traces, shows dashboards and raises alerts on guardrails and SLOs.

Workflow mapping.name: Workflow mapping
Workflow mapping.what: Diagrams who does what, in which order, with which tools — including the workarounds.

Golden signals.name: Golden signals
Golden signals.what: The four signals to watch for any user-facing system: latency, traffic, errors and saturation.
how: Measure latency of successful and failed requests separately
Measure saturation of the most constrained resource

rows: Time from email to draft order

Throughput analysis.name: Throughput analysis
Throughput analysis.what: Reading how much work a team actually finishes per period, and how variable that is.
how: Collect done items or points per sprint
Look at the range and trend

Spreadsheet model.name: Spreadsheet model
Spreadsheet model.what: A transparent model where assumptions, formulas and ranges are visible and adjustable.
how: Give every input a low / likely / high
Cite the source of each input

Problem statement canvas.name: Problem statement canvas
Problem statement canvas.what: A one-page template that forces the who, the problem, why it matters and the evidence into one place.

items: When and where does it happen?
Why does it matter — to them and to us?

Problem statement review.name: Problem statement review
Problem statement review.what: A peer check that every clause of a problem statement is backed by evidence and free of solutions.
how: Read the statement clause by clause
For each clause, find the evidence

rows: Describes the problem, not a solution

Fall in love with the problem.name: Fall in love with the problem
Fall in love with the problem.what: Stay attached to the problem and the user, not to the first solution you thought of.
how: Restate the problem before discussing solutions
Judge solutions by how well they solve it
Be ready to drop a favourite solution

Requirements traceability.name: Requirements traceability
Requirements traceability.what: Linking each requirement to its source and to what satisfies and verifies it, in both directions.
how: Link up: requirement → need → outcome → brief

Build / buy / partner.name: Build / buy / partner
Build / buy / partner.what: A structured comparison of building a capability in-house, buying an existing product, or partnering with someone who has it.
how: Describe the capability needed and how differentiating it is
Identify realistic buy and partner candidates
Score each option on the same criteria
Weigh total cost of ownership, not just licence or build cost
Recommend, with the trade-offs made explicit
Build / buy / partner.use: When a solution option exists outside the organisation.
pitfalls: Building commodity capabilities
Ignoring exit cost of a vendor

ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010.name: ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010
ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010.what: ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010:2022 Architecture description: what an architecture description must contain — stakeholders, concerns, viewpoints, views, correspondences and rationale.
how: Choose viewpoints that frame those concerns
Record correspondences between views and the rationale for decisions
says: An architecture description addresses identified stakeholders' concerns
Each view conforms to a viewpoint
Rationale for architecture decisions is recorded
ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010.applies: In DESIGN it shapes the architecture description and baseline (3.3.4): every view states its audience and concern; ADRs carry the rationale.

Ports and adapters.name: Ports and adapters
Ports and adapters.what: Core logic talks to the outside world only through interfaces (ports); adapters implement them for each technology, so vendors can be swapped and tested in isolation.
how: Define the port in the core's language
Implement an adapter per external system
Test the core with fakes and the adapter with contract tests

items: Vendor X, ERP import API, mailbox

Architecture review.name: Architecture review
Architecture review.what: Architects review an approach against principles, quality attributes and the existing landscape.

Don't build what you can buy.name: Don't build what you can buy
Don't build what you can buy.what: Build only what differentiates; buy or reuse the rest.
how: Check buy and partner options first

donts: Build what the market already sells cheaply

Weighted scoring.name: Weighted scoring
Weighted scoring.what: Scores options against weighted criteria so trade-offs are explicit and comparable.

Trade-off analysis.name: Trade-off analysis
Trade-off analysis.what: Compares options across weighted criteria to make the trade-offs explicit.
how: Discuss what you give up with each

Thin vertical slice.name: Thin vertical slice
Thin vertical slice.what: A story that cuts through every layer — UI, logic, data, integration — to deliver a small piece of working behaviour end to end.
how: Pick the thinnest path a user can use
pitfalls: Horizontal 'backend first' stories that deliver nothing usable

k6.name: k6
k6.what: An open-source load-testing tool scripted in JavaScript, with thresholds that pass or fail a run.

Technology radar.name: Technology radar
Technology radar.what: Places technologies in rings — adopt, trial, assess, hold — so options are judged against the organisation's stance.
how: Group technologies by quadrant (techniques, tools, platforms, languages)
Place each in a ring with a short rationale

items: Proceed with caution — don't start new work

Software composition analysis.name: Software composition analysis
Software composition analysis.what: Checking third-party components in the SBOM against known vulnerabilities and licence rules.

Weighted comparison.name: Weighted comparison
Weighted comparison.what: Scores each option against weighted criteria in a table.

Contract testing.name: Contract testing
Contract testing.what: Testing each side of an interface against a shared contract instead of standing up both systems together.
how: Write the contract (or let consumers write it)
Test the consumer against a stub from the contract
Verify the provider against the contract

ISO 31000.name: ISO 31000
ISO 31000.what: ISO 31000:2018 Risk management — Guidelines. A generic, non-certifiable international standard giving principles, a framework and a process for managing risk in any organisation or activity.
how: Set the scope, context and risk criteria for the activity
Identify risks — what could happen, why and how
Evaluate against criteria to decide what needs treatment
Treat, monitor and record; communicate throughout

rows: Value creation & protection: integrated, structured & comprehensive, customised, inclusive, dynamic, best available information, human & cultural factors, continual improvement
Leadership & commitment, integration, design, implementation, evaluation, improvement
Communication & consultation; scope, context & criteria; risk assessment; risk treatment; monitoring & review; recording & reporting

says: Risk is the effect of uncertainty on objectives
Risk management must be integrated into decision-making, not bolted on
Establish scope, external and internal context, and risk criteria before assessing risk
Communicate and consult with stakeholders throughout
Use the best available information and keep it current
ISO 31000.applies: In DISCOVER it frames the opportunity's context (1.1), bounds the scope of discovery as a risk activity (1.2 charter), and structures the risk and cost assessment and the Go / Kill decision (1.5).
ISO 31000.use: Any decision under uncertainty — especially investment and go / no-go decisions.
pitfalls: Treating it as a certification checklist (it isn't certifiable)

Decision record.name: Decision record
Decision record.what: A short, versioned record of a significant decision: its context, the options, the choice and its consequences.
how: Write it when the decision is made
Capture options considered, not just the winner
Never edit — supersede with a new record

items: What forces led to the decision

Cone of uncertainty.name: Cone of uncertainty
Cone of uncertainty.what: Estimates made early are uncertain by a wide factor; the range narrows as work is defined and done.
how: Narrow them by learning, not by pressure
Cone of uncertainty.use: Explaining why PLAN forecasts are ranges.

Retrospective.name: Retrospective
Retrospective.what: A structured, blameless look back at a piece of work to decide what to keep, stop and change — held for every outcome, including kills.
how: Set the scene: purpose, blameless rules
Gather data: timeline, what went well, what didn't, surprises
Generate insights: why did it happen?
Decide changes — each with an owner
Record in the learning log and close
Retrospective.use: At the end of discovery, whatever the decision, and after any stop.
pitfalls: Blaming people
Changes without owners

Decide explicitly.name: Decide explicitly
Decide explicitly.what: Every gate ends in a named decision with an owner and a rationale — never by default.

dos: Name the decision and its owner
donts: Let work drift on without a decision

Prefer ranges to false precision.name: Prefer ranges to false precision
Prefer ranges to false precision.what: Express estimates as ranges with confidence, not single numbers.

Three-point estimation.name: Three-point estimation
Three-point estimation.what: Estimating each work item as low, likely and high, with the basis for each, so uncertainty is visible instead of hidden in one number.
how: Break the work into items you can picture
For each, write low / likely / high
Note the basis — reference work, spike, guess
Sum as a range; flag items with the widest spread
Narrow wide items with a spike, not optimism
Three-point estimation.use: Estimating options in discovery and backlog items in PLAN.
pitfalls: Padding the likely value instead of widening the range
Presenting the likely value as a promise

Pre-mortem.name: Pre-mortem
Pre-mortem.what: Imagine the initiative failed; list the reasons; turn the likeliest into mitigations.

ADR log.name: ADR log
ADR log.what: The numbered, versioned set of ADRs in the repository, with status and links.

Risk register.name: Risk register
Risk register.what: A living list of risks with owner, rating and treatment, kept current as work proceeds.
how: Add each identified risk with its cause
Assign an owner and a treatment
Review at each gate; close or update

Technical risk assessment.name: Technical risk assessment
Technical risk assessment.what: Identifies and rates technical risks — complexity, integration, performance, skills.

Relative estimation.name: Relative estimation
Relative estimation.what: Sizing items against each other rather than in hours, which people do far more consistently.
how: Compare each item: bigger, smaller, about the same?

structure.text: Is this bigger or smaller than REF-B (5)? → pick the nearest size on 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13.

Relative estimation.source: Mike Cohn, Agile Estimating and Planning

ADR review.name: ADR review
ADR review.what: Peer review of an ADR before acceptance: real options, evidence, consequences, status.
how: Check consequences include the bad ones

BABOK.name: BABOK
BABOK.what: The Business Analysis Body of Knowledge: six knowledge areas that describe how analysts plan, elicit, analyse, manage and validate requirements.
how: Plan the analysis approach and stakeholder engagement
Analyse and define requirements and designs
Manage requirements through their life cycle
Monitor strategy and evaluate the solution
pitfalls: Producing every BABOK artifact regardless of size

ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148.name: ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148
ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148.what: ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148:2018 Systems and software engineering — Life cycle processes — Requirements engineering. Defines requirements processes and what a good requirement looks like.
how: Elicit stakeholder needs from all relevant stakeholders
Check every requirement against the quality characteristics
Manage requirements and traceability through the lifecycle

rows: Removing it would leave a real need unmet
At the right level of detail for its level
Needs nothing more to be understood
Accurately reflects the need and follows the agreed format

says: Stakeholder needs and requirements are distinct from system and software requirements
Requirements describe what is needed, not how to design it
Individual requirements and requirement sets have defined quality characteristics
Requirements must be traceable to their source
ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148.applies: In DISCOVER it keeps needs separate from solutions (1.2) and makes the validated problem and JTBD the raw stakeholder needs that PLAN turns into a requirements baseline.
ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148.use: From stakeholder needs in DISCOVER to the requirements baseline in PLAN.
pitfalls: Writing solutions disguised as requirements

Requirements workshop.name: Requirements workshop
Requirements workshop.what: A facilitated session where stakeholders and the team discover and agree requirements together.
how: Read the objective and outcomes aloud
Ask what must be true for each outcome
Ask what must never happen and who must not see what
Requirements workshop.use: Eliciting needs from a group quickly.
pitfalls: Letting the loudest voice write the list

Requirements baselining.name: Requirements baselining

Job stories.name: Job stories
Job stories.what: Writes needs as situation → motivation → outcome, grounded in observed situations.

Requirements management tool.name: Requirements management tool
Requirements management tool.what: Holds requirements with IDs, classes, versions, trace links and change history.
how: Link to needs, features and tests

Goal tree.name: Goal tree

Jobs-to-be-Done.name: Jobs-to-be-Done

Whiteboard.name: Whiteboard

Decision log.name: Decision log

WSJF.name: WSJF

Backlog tool.name: Backlog tool

Show each level on its own board

Scoring model.what: A shared sheet with criteria, weights and scores so ratings are consistent.

Scrum.name: Scrum

Kanban.name: Kanban

Reference stories.name: Reference stories

Deployment pipeline.name: Deployment pipeline

Branch protection.name: Branch protection
Branch protection.what: Repository rules that stop changes reaching main without review and green checks.

Secret scanning.name: Secret scanning

Artifact signing.name: Artifact signing
Artifact signing.what: Signing build artifacts in the pipeline and verifying the signature before deploy.

IaC tool.name: IaC tool
IaC tool.what: Declares infrastructure in code and shows a plan of changes before applying them.

CI/CD platform.name: CI/CD platform
CI/CD platform.what: Runs the pipeline on every change and keeps each run's logs, reports and artifacts.

Secrets manager.name: Secrets manager
Secrets manager.what: Stores, issues and rotates secrets, with access by identity and an audit log.

SBOM generator.name: SBOM generator
SBOM generator.what: Produces an SBOM from the source, lockfiles or container image during the build.

Twelve-Factor App.name: Twelve-Factor App
Twelve-Factor App.what: Twelve practices for building services that deploy cleanly to any environment: one codebase, explicit dependencies, config in the environment, dev/prod parity and more.

Keep dev, staging and production as similar as possible

Ephemeral environments.name: Ephemeral environments
Ephemeral environments.what: Short-lived, per-change environments created from code for each pull request and destroyed afterwards.

Drift detection.name: Drift detection
Drift detection.what: Comparing what is running with what the code declares, on a schedule, and alerting on differences.
how: Fix in code, never by hand

Git.name: Git
Git.what: Distributed version control: every change is a commit with an author, a message and a parent.

Continuous integration & delivery.name: Continuous integration & delivery
Continuous integration & delivery.what: Developers integrate small changes to the main branch many times a day; an automated pipeline builds, tests and keeps the software releasable at all times.

Quality gates.name: Quality gates

Trunk-based development.what: Everyone integrates small changes into one main branch at least daily; branches, if used, live hours, not weeks; main is always releasable.

Stop the line.name: Stop the line
Stop the line.what: When a serious defect or a broken pipeline appears, stop and fix it before adding more work.

Fast feedback.name: Fast feedback

Run the full suite on merge

Code hosting platform.name: Code hosting platform

Artifact repository.name: Artifact repository
Artifact repository.what: Stores versioned, immutable build artifacts with their SBOMs, signatures and provenance.

Short-lived credentials.name: Short-lived credentials
Short-lived credentials.what: Services get credentials that expire in minutes or hours, issued on demand to a workload identity, instead of long-lived stored secrets.

Remove long-lived keys where the provider allows

Secrets rotation.name: Secrets rotation
Secrets rotation.what: Replacing credentials and tokens on a schedule and immediately after any suspected exposure.

ISO/IEC 5230.name: ISO/IEC 5230
ISO/IEC 5230.what: ISO/IEC 5230:2020 Information technology — OpenChain Specification. Requirements for an open-source licence compliance programme.

A bill of materials is produced for supplied software
Licence obligations are identified and met

Hermetic builds.name: Hermetic builds
Hermetic builds.what: Builds that use only declared, pinned inputs and no network access during the build, so the same inputs always give the same output.

Fetch inputs before the build step

Automated dependency updates.name: Automated dependency updates
Automated dependency updates.what: A bot proposes dependency updates as small pull requests that run the full pipeline.

Dependency pinning.name: Dependency pinning
Dependency pinning.what: Locking every dependency to an exact version and hash so builds are reproducible and updates deliberate.

ISO/IEC/IEEE 26515.name: ISO/IEC/IEEE 26515
ISO/IEC/IEEE 26515.what: ISO/IEC/IEEE 26515:2018 Systems and software engineering — Developing information for users in an agile environment. How documentation is planned and produced inside iterations.

Re-plan change set.name: Re-plan change set
Re-plan change set.what: A change to a frozen sprint commitment is proposed as a set — added, removed, reason — and accepted by a person, keeping the history.

Sprint planning.name: Sprint planning
Sprint planning.what: The Scrum event that sets the sprint goal, selects Ready stories to meet it and plans how they will be built.

Daily scrum.name: Daily scrum
Daily scrum.what: A 15-minute daily event where the team inspects progress towards the sprint goal and adapts its plan.

Talk about the goal and blockers
Take blockers offline with the right people

Sprint review.name: Sprint review
Sprint review.what: The team shows done work to stakeholders, gathers feedback and adapts the backlog.

Sprint goal over sprint scope.name: Sprint goal over sprint scope
Sprint goal over sprint scope.what: The team commits to the sprint goal; the selected stories are the plan for reaching it.

donts: A goal that just lists the stories

Frozen commitments, explicit changes.name: Frozen commitments, explicit changes

donts: Rewrite the plan to match what happened

Sustainable pace.name: Sustainable pace
Sustainable pace.what: Plan for the pace the team can keep indefinitely; overtime hides problems and breeds defects.

Velocity-based forecasting.name: Velocity-based forecasting
Velocity-based forecasting.what: Forecasting how much the team will finish from the range of its recent sprints, adjusted for availability.

Story splitting.name: Story splitting
Story splitting.what: Breaking a large story into smaller ones that each still deliver value, using patterns such as workflow step, business rule, data variation and happy/unhappy path.

Keep each piece valuable and testable

Planning poker.name: Planning poker
Planning poker.what: Team estimation where everyone reveals an estimate at once and outliers explain their reasoning.

Burndown chart.name: Burndown chart
Burndown chart.what: A chart of work remaining in the sprint, day by day, against the ideal line.
how: Read the trend, not the day

WIP limits.name: WIP limits
WIP limits.what: A cap on how many items can be in a column at once, so the team finishes before starting.
how: Stop starting when the limit is reached

Sprint board.name: Sprint board
Sprint board.what: The visual board of the iteration backlog: stories and tasks moving from To do to Done.

Swarming.name: Swarming
Swarming.what: The team works together on the fewest stories at a time, finishing them before starting more.

Pull the next only when one is done

Task breakdown.name: Task breakdown
Task breakdown.what: Splitting a story into technical tasks of a day or less, including tests, instrumentation, migrations and docs.

Write for the reader.what: Documentation serves a specific reader with a specific need; write for them, not for completeness.
