dos: Start with what the reader needs to do

Docs are part of done.name: Docs are part of done
Docs are part of done.what: A change is not done until the documentation it affects is updated.

You build it, you run it.name: You build it, you run it
You build it, you run it.what: The team that builds a service is responsible for running it, so it builds it to be operable.

dos: Write the runbook as you build
donts: Throw it over the wall to operations

Done means releasable.name: Done means releasable
Done means releasable.what: Done means the increment could go to production now — reviewed, tested, documented, secure and deployable.

Keep a Changelog.name: Keep a Changelog
Keep a Changelog.what: A convention for a human-written changelog: versions newest first, changes grouped as Added, Changed, Deprecated, Removed, Fixed, Security.
how: Move them under the version at build

Runbook dry run.name: Runbook dry run
Runbook dry run.what: Walking through a runbook against a non-production environment to prove its steps work.

Docs site generator.name: Docs site generator
Docs site generator.what: Builds a documentation site from Markdown in the repository.

Monitoring & alerting.name: Monitoring & alerting
Monitoring & alerting.what: Collects metrics, logs and traces, shows dashboards and pages people when alert conditions hold.

Docs linting.name: Docs linting
Docs linting.what: Automated checks on documentation — broken links, style, spelling, missing sections — in the pipeline.

API-first design.name: API-first design
API-first design.what: The API contract is designed and agreed before the implementation, and everything else is generated or tested from it.

ISTQB test process.name: ISTQB test process
ISTQB test process.what: The test process body of knowledge from the International Software Testing Qualifications Board: planning, monitoring and control, analysis, design, implementation, execution and completion.
how: Plan — objectives, approach, entry and exit criteria
Analyse — what to test, from the test basis
Design — how to test: cases and data
ISTQB test process.use: As the backbone of a test approach, scaled down for agile teams.
pitfalls: Producing every document regardless of risk

Production-like staging.name: Production-like staging
Production-like staging.what: A pre-production environment configured like production — same build, same configuration shape, realistic integrations — so results there predict production.
how: Close the differences that matter to the risks under test
Deploy the same immutable build that will ship

rows: Results scaled with the capacity model

pitfalls: 'Works in staging' when staging differs in the thing being tested

Test environment management.name: Test environment management
Test environment management.what: Planning, provisioning, booking and controlling test environments so each test runs where it can prove what it claims.
how: Book and track who uses it

Test data management.name: Test data management
Test data management.what: Designing, creating, protecting and resetting the data tests need, so results are repeatable and lawful.
how: Name the data each case needs
Prefer synthetic; mask what is real
pitfalls: Copying production into test environments

Exhaustive testing is impossible.name: Exhaustive testing is impossible
Exhaustive testing is impossible.what: You cannot test everything; choose by risk and technique.

dos: Partition inputs and test the boundaries

Data masking.name: Data masking
Data masking.what: Replacing personal values in real data with realistic but fictitious ones, preserving format and relationships.

Synthetic data generation.name: Synthetic data generation
Synthetic data generation.what: Generating realistic test data from rules or models, with no real personal data.

Test management tool.name: Test management tool
Test management tool.what: Where cases, runs and coverage are kept and linked to requirements (e.g. Xray, TestRail, Azure Test Plans).

Test data generator.name: Test data generator
Test data generator.what: A script or tool that produces synthetic test data — here, synthetic PDF orders from ERP master data.

Defects cluster together.name: Defects cluster together
Defects cluster together.what: A small number of areas usually contain most defects; where you find some, look for more.

dos: Add exploratory sessions where defects cluster
donts: Spread effort evenly regardless of findings

Quality gate.name: Quality gate
Quality gate.what: A decision point with written exit criteria, judged on evidence, with three outcomes: pass, conditional pass with owned and tracked risks, or fail.
how: Decide, record, and name the owners of any conditions

rows: Gaps are low-risk, owned, dated and tracked
A criterion unmet and not acceptable

pitfalls: Conditions without owners or dates
Criteria rewritten at the gate

Continuous testing.name: Continuous testing
Continuous testing.what: Running automated tests at every stage of the pipeline so each build carries current evidence of its quality.
how: Run fast tests on every commit
Run system tests on every build to staging
Continuous testing.use: Functional and regression verification in CI.

Behaviour-driven development.name: Behaviour-driven development
Behaviour-driven development.what: Specifying behaviour as concrete examples in Given–When–Then that become automated acceptance tests.

CI pipeline.name: CI pipeline
CI pipeline.what: The automated pipeline that builds, tests and records evidence for every change (e.g. GitHub Actions, GitLab CI).

Site Reliability Engineering.name: Site Reliability Engineering
Site Reliability Engineering.what: Google's discipline of running services with software-engineering methods: reliability is defined by SLOs, the gap to 100% is an error budget to spend on change, and toil is engineered away.
how: Define SLIs from what users experience
Set SLOs below 100% and agree an error-budget policy
Alert on budget burn, not on causes
Respond to incidents with clear command and blameless postmortems
Cap toil and plan capacity ahead of demand

rows: A shared, numeric definition of 'reliable enough'
A rule for choosing between shipping and fixing
Fast restore and learning without blame

Site Reliability Engineering.use: Any service people depend on — scaled down for small teams, never skipped.
pitfalls: Copying Google's tooling instead of its practices
SLOs set at 100%
An 'SRE team' that just does operations
Site Reliability Engineering.source: Beyer et al., Site Reliability Engineering (2016) and The Site Reliability Workbook (2018)

Test against a named build.name: Test against a named build
Test against a named build.what: Every result names the immutable build it came from; evidence without a build version is evidence about nothing.
how: Stamp every run with the build version

dos: Re-run affected cases on rc3 after fixes in rc3
donts: Carry rc2 results over to rc3

Observability stack.name: Observability stack
Observability stack.what: Metrics, logs and traces that show how the system behaves under test (e.g. Grafana, Prometheus, OpenTelemetry).
how: Watch during load and fault tests

ISO/IEC 25059.name: ISO/IEC 25059
ISO/IEC 25059.what: ISO/IEC 25059 extends the ISO/IEC 25010 quality model for AI systems — adding characteristics such as functional correctness, robustness, user controllability and transparency.
how: Choose the AI-specific characteristics that matter
Evaluate them on held-out data, by segment

rows: Accuracy on poor scans and odd layouts
Low-confidence lines go to a person

says: AI systems need quality characteristics beyond the classic model
Correctness and robustness are evaluated, not assumed
ISO/IEC 25059.applies: In VERIFY it frames the extraction accuracy evaluation (5.3.4).

Golden dataset.name: Golden dataset
Golden dataset.what: A fixed, labelled, version-controlled data set with known correct outputs, used to measure accuracy and catch regressions.
pitfalls: Tuning on the evaluation set

Model evaluation.name: Model evaluation
Model evaluation.what: Measuring an ML component on held-out labelled data, by segment, with the metrics that matter for its use.

Given–When–Then.name: Given–When–Then
Given–When–Then.what: A structured form for acceptance criteria and scenarios: the context, the action, the observable outcome.
how: Then — the observable result, including what must not happen

structure.text: Given {context}, when {action}, then {observable outcome} — and not {wrong outcome}.

Quarantine flaky tests.name: Quarantine flaky tests
Quarantine flaky tests.what: Move a test that passes and fails on the same build out of the gating suite — with an owner, a fix date and interim coverage — rather than re-running until green.
how: Fix the cause and return the test
pitfalls: Quarantine as a graveyard — tests that never return

Exploratory testing.name: Exploratory testing
Exploratory testing.what: Simultaneous learning, test design and execution, guided by a charter and timeboxed — finding what scripted cases do not anticipate.
how: Write a charter: explore <area> with <resources> to discover <information>

structure.text: Explore {area} with {resources} to discover {information}.

Exploratory testing.use: Alongside scripted cases, focused on high-risk areas.

Regression testing.name: Regression testing
Regression testing.what: Re-running tests after a change to show that what worked still works.
how: Add the impacted areas by change analysis
Run the full suite before the gate
Retire tests that no longer earn their cost
pitfalls: Only ever adding tests — suites that take hours

Evidence-linked sign-off.name: Evidence-linked sign-off
Evidence-linked sign-off.what: A sign-off bound to specific evidence — run ids, links, a fingerprint of the results — that lapses when the evidence changes.
how: Invalidate the signature when a result or criterion changes
Evidence-linked sign-off.source: Squid delivery manual — 'Verified', 'Done' and 'Released' are computed, never asserted

Evidence, not claims.name: Evidence, not claims
Evidence, not claims.what: A result counts only when it carries evidence someone else can open — a run id and link, a record, a signature.
how: Link every pass to its run

dos: A passing case links a finished green CI run against the named build

Evidence, not claims.source: Squid delivery manual — linked evidence, not claims

Verified is not Done is not Released.name: Verified is not Done is not Released
Verified is not Done is not Released.what: Verified: every case passes in CI and the QA lead signed it. Done: verified and every DoD item has evidence. Released: a release decision said so. Each is computed from evidence; nobody asserts them.

dos: Compute each state from its evidence
donts: Call a story 'done' because it merged

Decision table testing.name: Decision table testing
Decision table testing.what: List combinations of conditions and the expected action for each, and test every column.

State transition testing.name: State transition testing
State transition testing.what: Model the states and transitions of an object and test valid and invalid transitions.

Playwright.name: Playwright
Playwright.what: An open-source browser automation framework for end-to-end tests across Chromium, Firefox and WebKit.

Error guessing.name: Error guessing
Error guessing.what: Use experience of typical mistakes to target likely defects.

Fix the cause, not the test.name: Fix the cause, not the test
Fix the cause, not the test.what: A failing or flaky test is information; change the code or the test's design, never just the expected result or the retry count.

dos: Fix the clock dependency that made a test flaky

Session-based test management.name: Session-based test management
Session-based test management.what: A way to make exploratory testing accountable: chartered, timeboxed sessions with a session sheet and a debrief.

Pesticide paradox.name: Pesticide paradox
Pesticide paradox.what: The same tests run repeatedly stop finding new defects; suites must be refreshed.
how: Add cases from escapes and exploration

dos: Add a case for every escaped defect
donts: Assume an old green suite still finds bugs

Pairwise testing.name: Pairwise testing
Pairwise testing.what: Cover every pair of parameter values with far fewer cases than all combinations.

Separation of duties.name: Separation of duties
Separation of duties.what: The person who approves a piece of work is not the person who produced it.
how: Assign an approver who is not one of them

dos: QA lead signs work they did not write
Risk owner, not the team, accepts residual risk
donts: Developers verifying and closing their own defects

Separation of duties.use: Verification sign-off, defect closure, risk acceptance.

CVSS.name: CVSS
CVSS.what: The Common Vulnerability Scoring System (FIRST, v4.0): a 0–10 score of a vulnerability's technical severity from its base, threat and environmental metrics.
how: Read the base score from the advisory
Combine with EPSS and known-exploited lists to prioritise
says: CVSS measures severity, not risk
Threat and environmental metrics refine the base score
CVSS.applies: In OPERATE it is one input to vulnerability triage (7.6.1) — never the only one.
pitfalls: Patching by CVSS alone

Penetration testing.name: Penetration testing
Penetration testing.what: An authorised, simulated attack by a skilled tester to find exploitable weaknesses scanners miss.
how: Agree scope and rules of engagement
Report findings by CVSS with reproduction
Penetration testing.use: Externally exposed or high-risk surfaces, before release.
Penetration testing.source: OWASP Web Security Testing Guide; PTES

Accessibility audit.name: Accessibility audit
Accessibility audit.what: A structured check of screens against WCAG using automated tools, manual inspection and assistive technologies, ideally with disabled users.

Risk is owned, never implied.name: Risk is owned, never implied
Risk is owned, never implied.what: Shipping with a known defect or unmet measure is a decision someone with authority makes, records and dates.

dos: Record each accepted risk with owner and date

Load testing.name: Load testing
Load testing.what: Applying realistic load to a production-like environment to prove it handles the expected peak and to find what fails first.
how: Model the peak from the forecast
pitfalls: Tiny synthetic documents that hide real cost

Chaos engineering.name: Chaos engineering
Chaos engineering.what: Experimenting on a system by injecting failures to build confidence that it withstands turbulent conditions.
how: Inject the fault with a small blast radius

Threat-model-driven testing.name: Threat-model-driven testing
Threat-model-driven testing.what: Deriving security tests from the threat model so every mitigation is attacked and verified.
how: Feed new threats back to the model

DAST.name: DAST
DAST.what: Dynamic application security testing: probing the running application from outside, as an attacker would.

Fuzz testing.name: Fuzz testing
Fuzz testing.what: Feeding large numbers of malformed or random inputs to find crashes and unsafe handling.
Fuzz testing.use: Parsers of untrusted input — such as PDFs.

Fault injection.name: Fault injection
Fault injection.what: Deliberately introducing a fault to check that alerts, runbooks and defences respond as intended.

Screen-reader testing.name: Screen-reader testing
Screen-reader testing.what: Completing tasks with a screen reader to check names, roles, states, order and announcements.
how: Note what is announced and where focus goes

OWASP ZAP.name: OWASP ZAP
OWASP ZAP.what: An open-source dynamic application security scanner.
how: Run baseline or full scans against staging

axe-core.name: axe-core
axe-core.what: An open-source accessibility rules engine used in browsers and automated tests.

OWASP Top 10.name: OWASP Top 10
OWASP Top 10.what: The OWASP list of the ten most critical web-application security risks, used as an awareness baseline.
how: Check the attack surface against each category
Make sure scanners and the pen test cover them
says: These categories cause most real-world breaches
OWASP Top 10.applies: In VERIFY it is the minimum coverage check for DAST and the pen test (5.3.2).
OWASP Top 10.use: A floor, not a ceiling — use ASVS for the full bar.

Semgrep.name: Semgrep
Semgrep.what: A static analysis tool for finding vulnerable code patterns.

Dependency scanner.name: Dependency scanner
Dependency scanner.what: A tool that checks dependencies against vulnerability databases (e.g. Dependabot, Trivy, OWASP Dependency-Check).

Keyboard-only testing.name: Keyboard-only testing
Keyboard-only testing.what: Completing every task without a mouse to check focus order, visibility and traps.

Screen readers.name: Screen readers
Screen readers.what: Assistive technology that reads interfaces aloud — NVDA and JAWS on Windows, VoiceOver on macOS and iOS.
how: Test key tasks with at least one

Restore drill.name: Restore drill
Restore drill.what: Restoring from backup into a clean environment and timing it, to prove recovery works.

Confusion matrix.name: Confusion matrix
Confusion matrix.what: A table of predicted versus actual outcomes, from which accuracy, precision and recall are read.
how: Count true / false positives and negatives

Defect tracker.name: Defect tracker
Defect tracker.what: Where defects are logged, triaged and tracked through their lifecycle (e.g. Jira, Linear, Azure Boards).

User acceptance testing.name: User acceptance testing
User acceptance testing.what: Real users run realistic business scenarios to decide whether they accept the solution for their work.
how: Draw scenarios from the users' jobs
Use real users and realistic data
Users decide: accept, accept with conditions, or not
pitfalls: The delivery team performing UAT on users' behalf

Site pilot.name: Site pilot
Site pilot.what: Running the solution for real work at one site or cohort first, measuring the outcome before wider rollout.
Site pilot.use: Validation that the right problem is solved.

Validate the outcome, not the output.name: Validate the outcome, not the output
Validate the outcome, not the output.what: Acceptance asks whether the problem is solved for users, measured against the value hypothesis — not whether features exist.

dos: Compare handling time before and during the pilot
donts: Accept because every feature was demonstrated

Absence-of-errors fallacy.name: Absence-of-errors fallacy
Absence-of-errors fallacy.what: A system with no known defects can still fail its users if it solves the wrong problem — verification is not validation.
how: Validate with users against the outcome

donts: Treat zero open defects as success

A metric below target is a signal, not a.name: A metric below target is a signal, not a defect
A metric below target is a signal, not a.what: If the capability works as specified and the outcome has not yet arrived, that is a product question for OPERATE and EVOLVE — not a defect for BUILD.

dos: Track outcome gaps as signals with an owner
donts: Raise a defect against an unmet business metric

A metric below target is a signal, not a.source: Squid delivery manual — signal vs defect

Before / after comparison.name: Before / after comparison
Before / after comparison.what: Comparing a measure on the same work before and after a change to isolate its effect.

Analytics.name: Analytics
Analytics.what: Measures real behaviour — visits, clicks, sign-ups, usage — for experiments and baselines.

Scheduling tool.name: Scheduling tool
Scheduling tool.what: Books sessions and sends reminders to participants and observers.

Defect lifecycle.name: Defect lifecycle
Defect lifecycle.what: The states a defect moves through and who may move it — so 'fixed' never means 'verified'.
how: Being fixed → Fixed — not yet verified
Re-tested on a new build → Verified → Closed
Or: Accepted — ships knowingly (owned) · Won't fix (decided)
pitfalls: Developers closing their own defects
'Accepted' silently treated as closed

Risk acceptance.name: Risk acceptance
Risk acceptance.what: A named owner, with authority for the rating, explicitly accepts a residual risk — with mitigation, conditions and an expiry.
how: State the risk and its residual rating
Show the mitigation is in place
Risk acceptance.use: Conditional passes at the Quality Gate.

Severity–priority triage.name: Severity–priority triage
Severity–priority triage.what: Separating how bad a defect is (severity — impact) from how soon it is fixed (priority — order), then deciding route and owner.
how: Set priority by impact, frequency and timing

rows: Critical — data loss, security breach, no workaround; blocks release
Major — core function wrong or unavailable; blocks release unless accepted

Defect triage.name: Defect triage
Defect triage.what: A short, regular review of new defects to confirm each one, set severity and priority, choose its route and owner, and decide fix, defer, accept or decline.
how: Is it a defect, a requirement issue, a change request or a signal?
pitfalls: Severity bargained down to pass the gate

Go / No-Go review.name: Go / No-Go review
Go / No-Go review.what: The meeting where the named release decider reads each release criterion against its evidence and decides go, no-go, or go with conditions — and records it.
how: Walk each criterion: met or not, with the artifact
For each unmet criterion: no-go, or a condition with an owner, evidence and date
Decide — a named person, a date, the outcome

rows: Each condition: accepted by, owner, evidence, due date, what it blocks
What failed, what must change, where work returns

pitfalls: Deciding in the room on evidence nobody has read
'Broadly yes' instead of yes or no
Conditions without owners
Go / No-Go review.source: Delivery manual — The Release Gate; ITIL 4 release management

Peer review of changes.name: Peer review of changes
Peer review of changes.what: A change is reviewed by someone other than its author, at an authority level that matches its risk — the lightweight alternative to a weekly change board.
how: Reviewer checks impact, risk, rollback and window
Peer review of changes.source: Forsgren et al., Accelerate — peer review outperforms external approval boards

A named person, a date, a decision.name: A named person, a date, a decision
A named person, a date, a decision.what: A release exists when an accountable person records go, no-go or go with conditions on a date — not when code reaches production.
how: Name the decider before the release
Record the decision with the date

Exclude explicitly, with reasons.name: Exclude explicitly, with reasons
Exclude explicitly, with reasons.what: What is not in the release is written down with the reason, and the people who asked for it are told before deployment.

dos: Record STY-122 and why it waits

Change risk assessment.name: Change risk assessment
Change risk assessment.what: Rates a change's likelihood of failure and its impact to choose its type, authority, window and safeguards.
how: Describe the change and what it touches
Add safeguards for the top risks

Release readiness review.name: Release readiness review
Release readiness review.what: A structured check, before the Go / No-Go, that every release criterion has an owner and an artifact, so the meeting only decides.
how: Flag gaps for conditions or no-go
Release readiness review.use: The day before every Go / No-Go.

Release checklist.name: Release checklist
Release checklist.what: A short, ordered checklist for the release window — pre-checks, steps, verification, communication.
how: Read it aloud in the window
Tick each item with the time

Release record system.name: Release record system
Release record system.what: The system of record for releases: picks, owners, evidence links, the decision, the production check and the close.

Change calendar.name: Change calendar
Change calendar.what: Shows planned changes, freezes and business peaks so windows don't collide.

Small, frequent releases.name: Small, frequent releases
Small, frequent releases.what: Smaller releases are easier to verify, decide on, roll back and learn from.
how: Release verified increments as soon as they are ready

dos: Ship a few stories at a time
donts: Batch a quarter's work into one release

Semantic versioning.name: Semantic versioning
Semantic versioning.what: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH version numbers that tell readers how big a change is.

Artifact registry.name: Artifact registry
Artifact registry.what: Stores built artifacts by immutable digest, with SBOM and provenance, for promotion between environments.

Single accountable owner.name: Single accountable owner
Single accountable owner.what: Every initiative and every decision has exactly one person who is answerable for the outcome.
how: Write down what they decide and what they escalate
pitfalls: Committees as owners

Limit the blast radius.name: Limit the blast radius
Limit the blast radius.what: Expose change so that a failure hurts as few users as possible, for as short a time as possible.

dos: Pilot with a few trained users
donts: Turn it on for everyone at once

ISO/IEC/IEEE 26514.name: ISO/IEC/IEEE 26514
ISO/IEC/IEEE 26514.what: ISO/IEC/IEEE 26514:2022 Systems and software engineering — Design and development of information for users. How to plan, structure and write user documentation.
how: Analyse the audience and their tasks
Plan the information set (task, concept, reference)
Keep it in step with the release

rows: Status codes in the Auto-filled queue

says: User information is designed from an analysis of users and their tasks
Instructions are task-oriented and tested with users
Information is accurate for the version of the software it describes
ISO/IEC/IEEE 26514.applies: In RELEASE it shapes the quick reference card, help articles and known-issues text (6.4.3) so they match the release and the users' tasks.
ISO/IEC/IEEE 26514.use: Writing user-facing documentation for any release.

Job story.name: Job story
Job story.what: A way of writing a need that captures the situation, the motivation and the expected outcome — without personas or solutions.
how: State the motivation in the user's terms

structure.text: When [situation], I want to [motivation], so I can [expected outcome].

Job story.use: To express validated needs from research.

Support enablement.name: Support enablement
Support enablement.what: Getting the service desk and support ready before users are exposed: briefing, knowledge articles, ticket routing, escalation and hypercare.
how: Write knowledge articles for the likely questions and known issues
Set up ticket categories and routing

Knowledge base.name: Knowledge base
Knowledge base.what: Searchable articles for agents and users, with ownership and review dates.

Expand / contract migration.name: Expand / contract migration
Expand / contract migration.what: Change a database in backward-compatible steps — expand (add), migrate, contract (remove) — so each deployment can be rolled back.
how: Expand: add new tables or columns; old code still works
Deploy code that writes both / reads new
Contract: remove the old structure in a later release
Expand / contract migration.use: Any release with a schema change.
pitfalls: Contracting in the same release as expanding — rollback becomes impossible

Blue-green deployment.name: Blue-green deployment
Blue-green deployment.what: Run two identical production environments; deploy to the idle one, test it, then switch traffic — and switch back to roll back.
how: Keep blue warm for instant rollback
Blue-green deployment.use: Services that need near-instant rollback of the whole version.
pitfalls: Database changes that only one colour can read
Blue-green deployment.source: Jez Humble & David Farley, Continuous Delivery (2010)

Rollback rehearsal.name: Rollback rehearsal
Rollback rehearsal.what: Running the deployment and its rollback end to end in staging, with the release build, and timing both.
how: Deploy the release build to staging with the production pipeline
Trigger each rollback path: flag off, redeploy previous
Check data and dependencies after rollback
Record times and fix what broke
pitfalls: Rehearsing with a different build or a hand-run script

Smoke testing.name: Smoke testing
Smoke testing.what: A short, automated set of checks run right after deployment that exercise the critical path end to end.
how: Pick the few paths that must work
Run immediately after deploy, before exposure
Fail the deployment if they fail

Roll back first, diagnose later.name: Roll back first, diagnose later
Roll back first, diagnose later.what: When a pre-agreed trigger fires, restore service first; investigate once users are safe.
how: Give on-call the right to roll back without asking

dos: Pull the flag on a breached threshold
donts: Debug in production while users suffer

Health checks.name: Health checks
Health checks.what: Endpoints and probes that report whether a service and its dependencies are working, used by the pipeline and the platform.

CI/CD pipeline.name: CI/CD pipeline
CI/CD pipeline.what: The automated pipeline that builds once, tests, and promotes the same artifact to staging and production, recording each run.
CI/CD pipeline.source: e.g. GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, Azure Pipelines

Feature-flag service.name: Feature-flag service
Feature-flag service.what: Manages runtime flags and their targeting, with an audit log.
how: Change flags with an audit trail

Dark launch.name: Dark launch
Dark launch.what: Deploy new code to production with users unexposed — exercising it with internal or shadow traffic before anyone depends on it.
how: Expose only when it is proven
Dark launch.use: Separating the risk of deployment from the risk of release.

On-call & paging tool.name: On-call & paging tool
On-call & paging tool.what: Routes alerts to the on-call person and records acknowledgement and escalation.

Ring deployment.name: Ring deployment
Ring deployment.what: Expose a change in concentric rings of users — from the team, to pilot users, to one site, to everyone — each ring a small go / no-go.
how: Define rings by risk and representativeness
Set entry criteria and soak per ring
Hold or roll back a ring without affecting others

items: Friendly, trained, close to the team

Ring deployment.use: Rollouts where users cluster naturally — by site, region or customer.
Ring deployment.source: Common practice (e.g. Microsoft safe deployment practices)

Soak period.name: Soak period
Soak period.what: A set time at a given exposure before the next step or the close, long enough for slow problems — leaks, queues, weekly patterns — to show.
how: Set the soak per ring before rollout
Soak period.use: Every ring and before closing the release.

Guardrail metrics.name: Guardrail metrics
Guardrail metrics.what: Defines the metrics that must not degrade during a rollout, each with a baseline, a pause threshold and a rollback threshold, captured before enablement.
how: Pick the few metrics that show harm
Wire them to dashboards and alerts
pitfalls: Only outcome metrics — harm shows too late
No baseline captured

Canary analysis.name: Canary analysis
Canary analysis.what: Compares the canary's metrics with a baseline or control group against thresholds set in advance to decide promote or roll back.
how: Choose metrics and thresholds before exposure
pitfalls: Moving the threshold after seeing the result

Synthetic monitoring.name: Synthetic monitoring
Synthetic monitoring.what: Sending scripted test transactions to the service to measure it when real traffic is low or unavailable.
how: Feed results into SLIs or alerts

Ready before exposed.name: Ready before exposed
Ready before exposed.what: Support, communications, documentation and training are ready for a group of users before that group is exposed.

dos: Train a site before its ring

Communication matrix.name: Communication matrix
Communication matrix.what: A grid of audiences against messages, channels and timing so nobody is missed.

Stakeholder communication plan.name: Stakeholder communication plan
Stakeholder communication plan.what: A plan of who needs to know what, when, through which channel and from whom — timed to the rollout.
how: Write what each needs to know and do
Stakeholder communication plan.use: Every release that changes how people work.

Train-the-trainer.name: Train-the-trainer
Train-the-trainer.what: Training a few super-users who then train their colleagues, close to the work and in their language.
how: Train them on staging with real-looking data
They train their teams before their ring
Train-the-trainer.use: Rollouts across several sites or languages.

Hypercare.name: Hypercare
Hypercare.what: A short, defined period after launch with extra support, daily check-ins and the building team on hand.
how: Set the length and exit criteria in advance
Staff it — engineers close to users
Exit when tickets and readings settle

items: Engineer on the floor, support lead
Tickets back to normal; no open Sev-1/2

Hypercare.use: Releases that change how people work.

DORA metrics.name: DORA metrics
DORA metrics.what: The DevOps Research and Assessment measures of software delivery performance: deployment frequency, lead time for changes, change failure rate and time to restore service (with reliability).
how: Measure the four keys continuously from the pipeline and incident data
Look at trends, not single values
Use worsening trends as evidence of debt and friction
DORA metrics.use: Spotting technical debt and delivery friction in EVOLVE; judging whether modernisation helped.
pitfalls: Using them to compare or rank teams
DORA metrics.source: Forsgren, Humble & Kim, Accelerate (2018); DORA reports

Production verification.name: Production verification
Production verification.what: Checking production against the things the release said would be true — NFRs, guardrails, success metrics and the consequences recorded in decisions — not just 'no errors'.
how: List every prediction: NFR targets, ADR consequences, success metrics
Record the result and route what doesn't match
Production verification.use: After deployment and through the soak period.
pitfalls: 'The release went fine' as the record

Operational acceptance.name: Operational acceptance
Operational acceptance.what: Operations formally accepts a service into live running once it has what it needs to run it: runbook, monitoring, alerts, SLOs, support model, known errors.
how: Agree the acceptance criteria with operations up front
Accept, accept with actions, or reject
Operational acceptance.use: Closing every release that changes a live service.
Operational acceptance.source: ITIL 4 — service validation & testing; release management

Error budget.name: Error budget
Error budget.what: The amount of unreliability an SLO allows (1 − target) over its window, spent deliberately on change and protected by a policy agreed in advance.
how: Compute the budget from the SLO: 99.5% over 28 days allows 0.5% bad events
Agree what happens at 75% and 100% spent
Freeze feature releases when it is spent; ship reliability fixes

items: e.g. 95% of lines need no correction

pitfalls: A policy nobody honours
Spending the budget on planned work by accident
Error budget.source: Google SRE Workbook, ch. 'Implementing SLOs' and 'Error budget policy'

Multi-window burn-rate alerting.name: Multi-window burn-rate alerting
Multi-window burn-rate alerting.what: Alerts on how fast an error budget is being spent, using a long window for significance and a short window to reset quickly, at several burn rates.
how: Pick the share of budget worth waking someone for (e.g. 2% in 1 h)
Convert to a burn rate (2% of 28 days in 1 h ≈ 14.4×)
Require both the long window (1 h) and a short window (5 min) to exceed it
Add a slower page (6× over 6 h) and a ticket (1× over 3 days)
pitfalls: Threshold alerts on raw error rates
One window only — slow to reset

Service level management.name: Service level management
Service level management.what: Agreeing measurable service levels with the people who rely on a service, monitoring them and reporting honestly.

On-call rotation.name: On-call rotation
On-call rotation.what: A schedule that shares responsibility for responding to pages, with escalation and limits that keep people rested.
pitfalls: One hero always on call
Unpaid, unrested on-call

Alert on symptoms, not causes.name: Alert on symptoms, not causes
Alert on symptoms, not causes.what: Page on user-visible symptoms (budget burn), and leave causes to dashboards and diagnosis.

donts: Page for every high CPU reading

RED method.name: RED method
RED method.what: For request-driven services, measure Rate, Errors and Duration of requests.

USE method.name: USE method
USE method.what: For every resource, check Utilisation, Saturation and Errors.

Burn-rate calculation.name: Burn-rate calculation
Burn-rate calculation.what: How fast an error budget is being spent relative to spending it exactly over the window.
how: Burn rate = observed error rate ÷ (1 − SLO)
Budget spent in time t = burn rate × t ÷ window

OpenTelemetry.name: OpenTelemetry
OpenTelemetry.what: An open standard and toolkit for generating and exporting traces, metrics and logs with consistent names.

Monitoring platform.name: Monitoring platform
Monitoring platform.what: Where metrics, SLIs, SLOs and alerts live.

Paging tool.name: Paging tool
Paging tool.what: Routes alerts to the on-call person and escalates if unanswered.

Hope is not a strategy.name: Hope is not a strategy
Hope is not a strategy.what: Reliability comes from targets, measurement and tested plans — not from expecting things to be fine.
how: Test the plan before you need it

donts: Assume last year's capacity will do

Runbook.name: Runbook
Runbook.what: A per-service operating guide: what each alert means, what to check first and which safe mitigations to apply.
pitfalls: Runbooks that describe the system instead of what to do

Dashboards as code.name: Dashboards as code
Dashboards as code.what: Defining dashboards and their queries in version control so they are reviewed, reproducible and kept in step with the service.
how: Store dashboard definitions in the repository
Dashboards as code.use: Any service with more than one dashboard.

Dashboard tool.name: Dashboard tool
Dashboard tool.what: Builds and shares dashboards from monitoring data.

Every alert is actionable.name: Every alert is actionable
Every alert is actionable.what: If a page needs no action, it shouldn't page.
how: Each alert names a runbook step

dos: Delete or downgrade alerts nobody acts on

Operations review.name: Operations review
Operations review.what: A regular meeting that looks at the whole service at once — SLOs, incidents, problems, support, capacity, cost, security — and ends each item in a decision.
how: Decide: monitor, problem, requirement or improvement
pitfalls: Status meeting with no decisions

Signals are not defects.name: Signals are not defects
Signals are not defects.what: A metric below target is a product signal, not a bug: the capability works and the outcome hasn't arrived yet. Defects break a stated criterion.
how: Ask: which criterion does this break?
If none, route it as a signal or requirement

dos: Route signals to the product owner and EVOLVE
File defects against a named criterion
donts: Send engineers to 'fix' behaviour that meets its specification

Trend analysis.name: Trend analysis
Trend analysis.what: Looking at incidents, contacts and metrics over time to find patterns before they become outages.
Trend analysis.use: Proactive problem management and budget reviews.

Change correlation.name: Change correlation
Change correlation.what: Lining up when a problem started against recent deployments, flag changes, config and vendor events.

Incident Command System.name: Incident Command System
Incident Command System.what: A role-based way of running an emergency: one commander, named functional leads and a common language, adapted from emergency services to IT incidents.
how: Delegate operations, communications and planning to named leads
Keep a single channel and a scribe
Incident Command System.use: Every major incident — Sev-1 and Sev-2 — and security incidents.
pitfalls: Commander debugging instead of commanding
Silent hand-overs
Incident Command System.source: FEMA ICS; adapted in Google SRE, PagerDuty incident response

Severity matrix.name: Severity matrix
Severity matrix.what: A table that sets incident severity from business impact and says what each severity triggers.
how: Define each severity in business terms
State the triggers: commander, cadence, postmortem

rows: Intake stopped or wrong goods shipped
Wrong orders caught, or site degraded > 30 min

pitfalls: Severity by technical symptom instead of user impact

Feature-flag kill switch.name: Feature-flag kill switch
Feature-flag kill switch.what: A runtime flag that turns a feature or path off — fully or for one segment — without a deployment.
how: Wrap risky features in flags with a safe 'off' state
Allow targeting by site, customer or input source
Feature-flag kill switch.use: The first, most reversible mitigation in an incident.
pitfalls: Flags never cleaned up

Status page.name: Status page
Status page.what: A single place where users and stakeholders see current service status and incident updates.
how: Post at declaration for user-visible incidents

Blameless Postmortems.name: Blameless Postmortems
Blameless Postmortems.what: A written review of an incident that explains how the system allowed it to happen, assumes people acted reasonably with what they knew, and produces owned actions.
how: Find contributing factors in the system
Blameless Postmortems.use: Every Sev-1/2 incident, near misses and big budget burns.
pitfalls: 'Human error' as a root cause
Actions never done
Blameless Postmortems.source: Google SRE book, 'Postmortem culture'; John Allspaw

Restore first, diagnose later.name: Restore first, diagnose later
Restore first, diagnose later.what: In an incident, stop the user harm by the safest means first; the root cause can wait for the postmortem.

dos: Flag off, roll back, fail over
donts: Debug in production while users wait

Blame the system, not the person.name: Blame the system, not the person
Blame the system, not the person.what: People act reasonably with what they know; failures come from systems that allow mistakes.
how: Ask how the system allowed it

donts: Name a person as the root cause

Declare early.name: Declare early
Declare early.what: When in doubt, declare an incident — downgrading is cheap, a late declaration is expensive.
how: Declare on suspicion of user impact

Incident triage.name: Incident triage
Incident triage.what: Quickly deciding what a signal is — incident, request, defect, feedback or noise — and how urgent.
Incident triage.use: Detection, the service desk and security alerts.

Timeline reconstruction.name: Timeline reconstruction
Timeline reconstruction.what: Rebuilding what happened, minute by minute, from logs, alerts, chat and records.
how: Mark decisions and what was known then

Incident channel.name: Incident channel
Incident channel.what: A dedicated chat channel or bridge per incident, with the timeline kept in it.

Service desk tool.name: Service desk tool
Service desk tool.what: Records contacts, requests, incidents and problems, with queues and SLAs.

Known-error database.name: Known-error database
Known-error database.what: A searchable store of known errors — problems with a documented cause or symptom and a tested workaround — kept until the fix is verified.
how: Record the workaround and its cost
Link the problem record and KB article
Known-error database.use: Problem management and the service desk.
pitfalls: Known errors never retired

Impact–urgency matrix.name: Impact–urgency matrix
Impact–urgency matrix.what: Priority set by combining how much harm an issue causes with how soon it gets worse.

Graceful degradation.name: Graceful degradation
Graceful degradation.what: Designing a service to keep doing its core job, with less, when part of it fails or is overloaded.
how: Decide what to drop first under stress
Show users the degraded state honestly

Circuit Breaker.name: Circuit Breaker
Circuit Breaker.what: Stops calling a failing dependency for a while so failures don't cascade, then tries again carefully.
how: Open the circuit above a threshold — fail fast
After a pause, let a trial request through (half-open)
Circuit Breaker.use: Calls to the OCR API or ERP import API.

Change enablement.name: Change enablement
Change enablement.what: Getting changes into production safely and quickly by matching the scrutiny to the risk: standard changes pre-approved, normal changes assessed, emergency changes expedited.
how: Classify the change: standard, normal or emergency
Change enablement.use: Every production change, including operational ones.
pitfalls: One heavy board for every change

Fault tree analysis.name: Fault tree analysis
Fault tree analysis.what: Works down from an undesired event through AND / OR gates to the combinations of causes that produce it.
how: Add the immediate causes with AND / OR

items: Wrong quantity reaches a draft order
Misread digit · wrong layout · bad import
Low-res input AND over-confident score AND single threshold

One backlog, one order.name: One backlog, one order
One backlog, one order.what: Problem fixes, features and improvements compete in the same ordered product backlog.
how: Rank fixes with the same method as features

dos: Show the cost of problems beside feature value
donts: Keep a side queue of fixes nobody ranks

Knowledge-Centred Service.name: Knowledge-Centred Service
Knowledge-Centred Service.what: The Consortium for Service Innovation's method (KCS v6) for creating and improving knowledge as a by-product of solving issues.
how: Capture in the user's words while solving
Reuse: search first, link every contact to an article
Improve: fix articles as you use them
Knowledge-Centred Service.use: Any service desk that answers the same questions twice.
pitfalls: Writing articles after the fact, or never
One author bottleneck
Knowledge-Centred Service.source: Consortium for Service Innovation, KCS v6

Shift-left.name: Shift-left
Shift-left.what: Moving resolution to the earliest point — self-service, then tier 1 — by giving users and agents the knowledge and tools to solve issues themselves.
how: Turn it into KB articles or request models
pitfalls: Shifting work without the knowledge to do it

Tiered support.name: Tiered support
Tiered support.what: Support organised in tiers of increasing specialism, with clear hand-offs and the aim of solving as early as possible.
how: Tier 1: service desk — KB, requests, triage
Tiered support.use: Any service with more than a handful of users.
pitfalls: Tiers as walls — tickets bounced, not solved

Request model.name: Request model
Request model.what: A pre-defined, repeatable way to fulfil one type of service request, with its approvals, steps and time.

Least Privilege.name: Least Privilege
Least Privilege.what: Every person and system gets only the access it needs, for only as long as it needs it.

dos: Remove leavers the day they leave

Identity provider.name: Identity provider
Identity provider.what: Central accounts, groups and tokens with audit logs.

Capture before judging.name: Capture before judging
Capture before judging.what: Record ideas faithfully first; evaluate them later.

dos: Write down exactly what was said
donts: Dismiss or rewrite ideas on arrival

Verbatim capture.name: Verbatim capture
Verbatim capture.what: Writes the idea down word-for-word as the requester said it, before anyone interprets it.

FinOps Framework.name: FinOps Framework
FinOps Framework.what: The FinOps Foundation's framework for managing the cost of cloud and technology services as a shared responsibility between engineering, finance and the business.
how: Inform — allocate costs and show who spends what
Optimise — rightsize, remove waste, use commitments
Operate — set targets, review regularly, improve
FinOps Framework.use: Whenever run cost is material or growing with usage.
pitfalls: Cutting cost without looking at value
Finance-only ownership

Headroom policy.name: Headroom policy
Headroom policy.what: A rule for how much spare capacity every resource must have at forecast peak.
how: Set headroom per resource (e.g. 30% at peak hour)
Act when forecast headroom falls below policy

Showback.name: Showback
Showback.what: Showing each service or team the costs it incurs, without charging them, so cost becomes visible and owned.
how: Allocate costs by tags and rules

Cost allocation tagging.name: Cost allocation tagging
Cost allocation tagging.what: Tagging every resource with service, environment and owner so costs can be allocated automatically.

Unit cost over total cost.name: Unit cost over total cost
Unit cost over total cost.what: Judge run cost per unit of value (per order), not only in total — a growing bill can mean a growing business.
how: Report cost per order beside value per order

dos: Track unit cost and value together
donts: Cut total cost without looking at value

Demand forecasting.name: Demand forecasting
Demand forecasting.what: Estimating future demand from history and business drivers as ranges by scenario.

Activity-based costing.name: Activity-based costing
Activity-based costing.what: Allocating shared costs to services by the activities that drive them.
Activity-based costing.use: Cost to serve with shared platforms.

Little's Law.name: Little's Law
Little's Law.what: In a stable system, items in the system = arrival rate × time in the system (L = λW).

Unit economics.name: Unit economics
Unit economics.what: Cost and value per unit of service — here, per order.

Rightsizing.name: Rightsizing
Rightsizing.what: Matching resource size and tier to actual use.

Load-test tool.name: Load-test tool
Load-test tool.what: Generates realistic load and records how the service responds.

Cloud cost explorer.name: Cloud cost explorer
Cloud cost explorer.what: Shows cloud and vendor spend by tag, service and time.

NIST Cybersecurity Framework.name: NIST Cybersecurity Framework
NIST Cybersecurity Framework.what: NIST's framework (CSF 2.0) organising cybersecurity outcomes into six functions: Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover.
how: Govern — set strategy, roles and policy
Identify — know assets, risks and weaknesses
Protect — safeguards such as access control and patching
Respond — contain and act on incidents
NIST Cybersecurity Framework.use: Organising security operations so nothing falls between the functions.
pitfalls: Treating it as a compliance checklist

NIST SP 800-61.name: NIST SP 800-61
NIST SP 800-61.what: NIST Special Publication 800-61 — Computer Security Incident Handling Guide (Rev. 3, 2025 aligns it with CSF 2.0): how to prepare for, detect, analyse, contain, eradicate and recover from security incidents.
how: Detect and analyse: triage alerts, confirm and scope
Post-incident activity: lessons learned, evidence retention
says: Incident handling is planned and practised before it is needed
Containment strategies are chosen by damage, evidence needs and service availability
Evidence is preserved and its chain of custody recorded
Lessons learned feed back into preparation
NIST SP 800-61.applies: In OPERATE it structures Respond to Security Incidents (7.6.3).
pitfalls: Destroying evidence while cleaning up

Detection as code.name: Detection as code
Detection as code.what: Security detection rules written, reviewed, tested and deployed like code.
how: Test each rule against simulated attacks and normal traffic
pitfalls: Rules edited live with no test

Patch management.name: Patch management
Patch management.what: Applying security and stability patches on a schedule set by risk, verified and recorded.

Access recertification.name: Access recertification
Access recertification.what: Owners periodically confirming that every account and privilege is still needed, and removing what isn't.
pitfalls: Rubber-stamping

Game day.name: Game day
Game day.what: A planned exercise that simulates a failure or attack in a controlled way to test people, runbooks and detections.
how: Record what worked and what didn't

Assume breach.name: Assume breach
Assume breach.what: Design operations as if an attacker is already inside: detect, limit and recover, not only prevent.

Risk-based vulnerability prioritisation.name: Risk-based vulnerability prioritisation
Risk-based vulnerability prioritisation.what: Ordering vulnerability fixes by real risk — exploitability, exposure and impact — not by CVSS score alone.
how: Is it exploited in the wild (KEV) or likely to be (EPSS)?

Threat-informed detection.name: Threat-informed detection
Threat-informed detection.what: Choosing what to detect from the threats the threat model rates highest and the techniques attackers use.

EPSS.name: EPSS
EPSS.what: The Exploit Prediction Scoring System (FIRST): the probability a vulnerability will be exploited in the next 30 days.
how: Combine with CVSS, exposure and known-exploited status

Vulnerability scanner.name: Vulnerability scanner
Vulnerability scanner.what: Scans images, dependencies and hosts for known vulnerabilities against the SBOM.

SIEM.name: SIEM
SIEM.what: Security information and event management: collects security logs, runs detections and supports investigation.

Secrets vault.name: Secrets vault
Secrets vault.what: Stores secrets with access control, expiry and rotation.

HEART framework.name: HEART framework
HEART framework.what: Google's framework for user-centred metrics: Happiness, Engagement, Adoption, Retention and Task success, each traced from goals to signals to metrics.
how: Pick the HEART categories that matter for this change
Find the signals that show progress
Turn signals into metrics you can track
HEART framework.use: Choosing user-experience metrics for outcome measurement.
pitfalls: Using all five categories everywhere

Leading & lagging indicators.name: Leading & lagging indicators
Leading & lagging indicators.what: Pairs lagging outcome measures (the result) with leading indicators that move earlier and predict it, plus guardrails that must not get worse.
how: Find a leading indicator that moves first
Read leading indicators often, outcomes at the by-date
pitfalls: Leading indicators that don't predict the outcome

Outcome review.name: Outcome review
Outcome review.what: A scheduled review at the by-date the success criteria set, where readings are compared with targets and the owner decides to continue, change course or stop — and records it.
how: Collect the readings for every criterion
Show each against baseline and target
Decide: continue, change course or stop
Record the decision and the next reading date
Outcome review.use: At every success-criterion by-date and before each portfolio review.
pitfalls: Reviewing only the metrics that look good
No decision at the end

Measure what was promised.name: Measure what was promised
Measure what was promised.what: Judge a change against the success criteria and value hypothesis it was funded on — not against whatever metric looks best now.
how: Start the review from the opportunity brief
Report every criterion, met or not

dos: Report every criterion from the brief
Keep the original targets and dates
donts: Swap in a new metric that looks better
Move the target after the fact

Separate recording from judging.name: Separate recording from judging
Separate recording from judging.what: Whoever records the readings does not judge them, so numbers are not shaped to a conclusion.
how: Name a recorder and a different judge for each criterion

donts: Let the team that built it grade its own outcome alone

Comparison group.name: Comparison group
Comparison group.what: Reads an outcome against a comparable group that did not get the change (or got it later) to separate the change's effect from seasonality and other causes.
how: Find a comparable unaffected group (a site not yet rolled out)
Measure both over the same period
State the confounders you could not remove
Comparison group.use: Rollout by site gives a natural comparison group.
pitfalls: Groups that differ in more than the change

Cohort analysis.name: Cohort analysis
Cohort analysis.what: Groups users or orders by when they started (or a shared trait) and follows each group over time to see adoption and retention.

Outcome dashboard.name: Outcome dashboard
Outcome dashboard.what: A live view of each success criterion against its baseline and target, by segment, with the data source behind each tile.
how: Link each tile to its query

OKR tracker.name: OKR tracker
OKR tracker.what: Where objectives and key results are published and progress tracked.

Pre-registered experiments.name: Pre-registered experiments
Pre-registered experiments.what: The hypothesis, metric and success threshold are written down before the experiment runs, so results can't be reinterpreted afterwards.
how: Read the result against the threshold

Affinity clustering.name: Affinity clustering
Affinity clustering.what: Groups individual observations into themes from the bottom up, letting patterns emerge from the data.
how: Silently group notes that belong together
Name each group with a statement, not a topic
Group the groups into higher-level themes

items: Name each cluster as an insight

Voice of the customer programme.name: Voice of the customer programme
Voice of the customer programme.what: A standing way of gathering feedback from every channel — support, surveys, sales, interviews, in-product — into one place with consistent tags.
how: List every channel and its owner
Export into one inventory every period
pitfalls: Listening only to the loudest customer

Closing the feedback loop.name: Closing the feedback loop
Closing the feedback loop.what: Telling the people who gave feedback what was learned and what will — or won't — happen.
how: Decide what will happen for each theme
Tell the givers, in their channel
Track whether feedback volume and quality hold up

structure.text: You said … · We found … · We will / won't … because … · Tell us more at …

pitfalls: Only replying when the answer is yes

Every insight reaches a backlog.name: Every insight reaches a backlog
Every insight reaches a backlog.what: An insight is finished only when it is an item in a backlog or has been dropped with a reason.

dos: Give every insight a route and an owner
donts: Leave insights in a slide deck

Insight synthesis.name: Insight synthesis
Insight synthesis.what: Combines qualitative feedback with quantitative usage and operational data to form insights each backed by more than one kind of evidence.
how: Quantify each theme from usage and ops data
Peer-review and discard what doesn't hold

structure.text: We observed … (evidence) because … (cause), so we believe … (implication). Confidence: …

Insight synthesis.use: Turning a period's signals into insights.
pitfalls: One vivid anecdote becoming an insight

Thematic analysis.name: Thematic analysis
Thematic analysis.what: A systematic way of finding, reviewing and naming patterns in qualitative data.

NPS / CSAT.name: NPS / CSAT
NPS / CSAT.what: Short standard surveys: Net Promoter Score (likelihood to recommend, 0–10) and Customer Satisfaction (rating of a recent interaction).
how: Track trend and verbatims, not just the score

items: How likely are you to recommend …? / How satisfied were you with …?
What is the main reason for your score?

pitfalls: Chasing the score instead of the reasons

Research repository.name: Research repository
Research repository.what: One searchable home for research notes, recordings and insights, linked to the decisions they informed.
how: Store every study in the same structure

Continuous discovery.name: Continuous discovery
Continuous discovery.what: The product trio talks to customers every week and runs small assumption tests continuously, instead of doing discovery as a one-off phase.
how: Interview at least one customer a week
Synthesise into opportunities on an opportunity solution tree
Pick a target opportunity and generate solutions
Test the riskiest assumptions with small experiments
Continuous discovery.use: As the habit behind all discovery work.

Observe behaviour, not opinion.name: Observe behaviour, not opinion
Observe behaviour, not opinion.what: Trust what people do over what they say they would do.
how: Ask about past events, not hypotheticals

dos: Ask 'tell me about the last time…'

Research synthesis.name: Research synthesis
Research synthesis.what: Turns raw research notes into themes, insights and implications others can act on.

Synthesis board.name: Synthesis board
Synthesis board.what: A digital board for clustering research notes into themes and insights.

ISO/IEC 14764.name: ISO/IEC 14764
ISO/IEC 14764.what: ISO/IEC/IEEE 14764:2022 Software engineering — Software life cycle processes — Maintenance. Classifies maintenance and describes how to plan and run it.
how: Classify each change: corrective, preventive, adaptive, perfective
Analyse the problem or modification and its impact
Implement, review and accept the change
Plan migration and retirement when the software ends

rows: Fix latent faults before they fail
Keep working in a changed environment

says: Maintenance includes adaptive and preventive work, not only bug fixes
Every modification is analysed for impact before it is made
Migration and retirement are maintenance activities with their own plans
ISO/IEC 14764.applies: In EVOLVE it classifies tech-debt items and modernisation (8.3) and the migration part of retirement (8.5).
ISO/IEC 14764.use: Classifying and planning maintenance and modernisation work.
pitfalls: Treating all maintenance as 'bug fixing'

Idea backlog.name: Idea backlog
Idea backlog.what: The single list where ideas are logged, de-duplicated and tracked.

SRE.name: SRE
SRE.what: Site Reliability Engineering: runs services with explicit service-level objectives and error budgets, and treats toil and reliability work as engineering to be reduced.
how: Spend the error budget on change; freeze when it is gone
Feed postmortem actions into the backlog
SRE.use: In EVOLVE, error-budget burn and toil are evidence of reliability debt.
pitfalls: 100% targets
Postmortem actions that never reach a backlog
SRE.source: Beyer et al., Site Reliability Engineering (Google, 2016)

Strangler fig.name: Strangler fig
Strangler fig.what: Replaces a legacy component gradually: new code grows around the old behind the same interface, traffic moves over slice by slice, and the old part is removed when nothing uses it.
how: Put a routing facade in front of the legacy part
Build one slice in the new implementation
Route that slice to the new code; compare
Repeat until nothing reaches the old code
Strangler fig.use: Modernising a component without a big-bang rewrite.
pitfalls: Never finishing — two systems forever

Parallel run.name: Parallel run
Parallel run.what: Runs the old and the new implementation side by side on the same inputs and compares outputs before switching over.
how: Feed both implementations the same inputs
Use the old output; log the new
Switch when mismatches stay at zero for the agreed period
Parallel run.use: Migrations and modernisations where correctness matters — such as order data.
pitfalls: Comparing only counts, not content

Capacity allocation for debt.name: Capacity allocation for debt
Capacity allocation for debt.what: Reserves a fixed share of each team's capacity for debt paydown and improvement, so it happens in flow instead of waiting for a 'clean-up project'.
how: Agree a share (often 10–20%) with the product owner
Fill it from the ranked debt register
Review the share quarterly against interest trends

structure.text: Each sprint, …% of capacity goes to the top-ranked debt and improvement items.

pitfalls: Raiding the allocation for features under pressure

Make debt visible.name: Make debt visible
Make debt visible.what: Technical debt is managed only when it is written down, quantified and ranked alongside features.

dos: Record interest in time or risk
donts: Ask for 'a refactoring sprint' with no case

7 Rs of modernisation.name: 7 Rs of modernisation
7 Rs of modernisation.what: A menu of options for each component: retain, retire, rehost, replatform, refactor, re-architect, replace (repurchase).
how: Choose one R per component, with a reason
Record the choice in the modernisation plan

rows: Move with small changes (e.g. new API version)

pitfalls: Re-architecting by default

Debt interest estimate.name: Debt interest estimate
Debt interest estimate.what: Estimates the ongoing cost of a debt item — extra effort, incidents, delay or risk per period — so it can be compared with the cost of fixing it.
how: Find where the debt costs time (each change, each incident, each onboarding)
Compare with the cost to fix
pitfalls: Precision theatre — ranges are fine

Tech-debt register.name: Tech-debt register
Tech-debt register.what: A maintained list of debt items with quadrant, interest, cost to fix, rank and plan.

Retire on purpose.name: Retire on purpose
Retire on purpose.what: Things are switched off deliberately — with users moved, data handled and costs removed — not left to decay.
how: Consider retire at every portfolio review

donts: Leave unused systems running 'just in case'
